unlisted_note_dispositions.explanation: The ḥataf form belongs to Miqraot Gedolot HaKeter’s reconstruction of Aleppo practice; the note’s explicit Leningrad form has sheva.
The historical Aleppo-question form וּשֲקָה is expressly rejected: sheva only.
Explicit Leningrad ḥataf pataḥ on resh; no corresponding list word.
The שִׁבֳּלִים vowel is intrinsic short-o; the source difference discussed here is dagesh on shin.
Intrinsic short-o in שִׁבֳּלִים; the note compares he pointing and dagesh on shin.
Intrinsic short-o in שִׁבֳּלִים; source uncertainty concerns dagesh on shin, not optional vocal-sheva marking.
Intrinsic short-o in שִׁבֳּלִים; the note’s uncertainty concerns dagesh on shin.
The note expressly says ḥataf qamats marks short qamats; source disagreement about the glyph is retained.
The ḥataf is assigned to British Library Or. 4445 and the Washington Pentateuch, with some editions; Aleppo/Leningrad attribution is not supplied.
Explicit surprisingly-equal Leningrad form has ḥataf pataḥ on vav; no corresponding list word.
The old question כמתאנֲנים is explicitly answered: sheva only.
Aleppo Sefer-question form is explicitly answered sheva only; a printed-edition form repeats the ḥataf quotation.
Leningrad ḥataf ḥiriq is explicitly uncertain: the blurred sign may be gaʿya instead.
Non-guttural yod ḥataf belongs only to Firkovich B17; the Leningrad he vowel is guttural.
Intrinsic short-o in the qere בָּמֳתֵי and the Aleppo spelling בָּמֳותֵי, as distinguished from the optional vocal-sheva policy.
Explicit Aleppo ḥataf pataḥ on resh; no corresponding list word.

Pointed Aleppo ketiv הָאֲוְרֲ֥נָה has a resh ḥataf, while the qere הָֽאֲרַ֥וְנָה has different letters/vowels. The note supplies no vowel-function statement; whether this is optional vocal-sheva marking is unresolved.
Pointed Aleppo ketiv אֲרַ֥נֳיה has a nun ḥataf qamats, while qere אֲרַ֥וְנָה differs. Neither a morphological exclusion nor a scoped omission is established.
The ḥataf form is assigned to Cairo, while Aleppo and Leningrad forms have sheva.
Printed editions and Cairo have the alternative qamats/pataḥ ḥataf forms; the note expressly says Aleppo and Leningrad have sheva.
Intrinsic short-o in אֶשְׁקֳטָה, including the Aleppo full spelling; the note’s issue is full spelling and absence of a qere annotation.
Intrinsic short-o in בָּמֳותֵי, with an explicit cross-reference to Deuteronomy32:13.
Contextual inference: ketiv לְזַוֲעָה transfers the qere לְזַעֲוָה guttural ayin’s vowel to vav in transposed letters. This does not establish an optional vocal-sheva ḥataf.
The quoted יֱהֹוִה belongs to a different verse (32:25) in a provenance paragraph; divine-name qere pointing is outside the list’s vocal-sheva purpose.

The list already lists a ḥataf qere וּֽזֳעָ֑קוּ, but the note expressly documents pointed ketiv וּֽזֳעָ֑קיּ. The manuscript qere vowel is not established by that note; retain the existing source-boundary question.
Breuer reports ḥataf in מִבֲּכִי; the note’s inspection instead suggests a stain or an erased pataḥ stroke leaving sheva. No definite omission follows.
The note expressly says ḥataf qamats marks short qamats.
The list already lists a ḥataf qere שׁוֹבֲב֑וּם, while the note documents pointed ketiv שׁוֹבֲב֑יּם. This remains a source-object boundary, rather than a newly omitted position.
The printed-edition ḥataf marks short qamats; it is not assigned to Aleppo or Leningrad.
The note expressly says ḥataf qamats marks short qamats.

The implicit Aleppo target שֱׁיְהֹוָה has reduced segol on the prefix shin; explicit Leningrad שֶׁיֲהֹוָה has the divine-name vowel on yod. Both forms are retained concretely. The ordinary prefix has segol, not sheva, and this is divine-name qere/function pointing rather than the list’s optional vocal-sheva marking.
Explicit Leningrad qoph ḥataf pataḥ; the list lists only the separate תלעג word at the same verse.
Explicit surprisingly-equal Leningrad ḥataf segol on shin; no corresponding list word.
The ḥataf is attributed to reconstructed Aleppo practice; Leningrad is explicitly quoted with sheva and the Aleppo manuscript is not explicitly extant here.

Intrinsic short-o in בַשִׁבֳּלִים; the note compares shin dagesh and meteg.
Intrinsic short-o in אֲלַקֳּטָה; the stated uncertainty concerns dagesh on qoph, not the function of its vowel.
Named Sassoon 1053, Cairo 13 and Sassoon 82 sources plus reconstructed Aleppo practice have ḥataf; Leningrad explicitly has none.
The explicit ḥataf belongs to St Petersburg EVR-II-B-55 and unspecified books, not the named Aleppo/Leningrad list sources.
Leningrad ḥataf pataḥ on yod is expressly uncertain; the note describes an indistinct unusual stroke.
Breuer supports Leningrad ḥataf; Dotan and the note retain doubt because an enlarged image does not show a clear pataḥ stroke.
The note expressly says ḥataf qamats marks short qamats.
